knowledge_checks.title: Active Recall: 1.2.2
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Which statement correctly distinguishes Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall correlation measures?
knowledge_checks.body: Select measure definitions and one inference caution.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Measures differ in what association they capture. Identity claims, causal proof, or PCA confusion are wrong.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Pearson linear; Spearman/Kendall rank; correlation ≠ causation.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Treating measures as identical or reading causation from r.

choices.label: Pearson measures linear association; Spearman and Kendall use ranks and suit monotone but nonlinear patterns and outlier resistance better in many skewed cases. A large coefficient does not prove causation.
Pearson, Spearman, and Kendall always give identical values because they are three names for the same formula.
A significant Pearson correlation proves that changing X causes Y to change in the observed direction.
Kendall is used only for PCA inputs; Pearson is used only after PCA scores are constructed.

knowledge_checks.title: Checkpoint: 1.2.2
knowledge_checks.prompt: Closed-book. Years licensed vs claim frequency: frequency is skewed with outliers; scatter looks roughly decreasing but nonlinear. Which statement is correct?
knowledge_checks.body: Choose correlation measure and state one limit of a large coefficient.
hints: Use the concept from this learning objective only.
knowledge_checks.explanation: Rank measures suit monotone nonlinear patterns with outliers. Neither Pearson-only nor causal claims follow from association alone.
knowledge_checks.model_answer: Spearman/Kendall preferred; refuse causation from correlation.
knowledge_checks.common_mistake: Pearson by default, causal inference from r, or PCA confusion.

choices.label: Prefer Spearman (or Kendall) because the relationship looks monotone but nonlinear and outliers can distort Pearson. A large coefficient still does not prove that changing years licensed causes frequency to change.
Use Pearson only because linear correlation is required whenever a scatter plot is drawn.
A strong negative Spearman correlation proves that reducing years licensed will reduce claim frequency.
Use Kendall because it measures variance explained by PC1, which is the correct bivariate association measure here.
